explanations.explanation: John says it right out loud: the dragon is "…that ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan…" That's one enemy wearing a whole drawer full of name tags. Whichever name you hear, John means the same one. The angel grabs him and doesn't ask which name he prefers.

Those two are names of false gods in the Old Testament. Dagon was a god of the Philistines, Israel's neighbors (Judges 16:23), and Baal was a false god too (1 Kings 18:21). John doesn't use either one here. He says the dragon is "…the devil and Satan…"

Bel and Nebo are Babylon's idols, and Isaiah mentions them (Isaiah 46:1). They're not the dragon's other names, though. John says the dragon is "…that ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan…" So the two names are the devil and Satan.

That's the one, friend. The angel had the key to the Abyss, and John says he "…threw him into the Abyss, shut it, and sealed it over him…" Key, chain, shut, sealed. That angel did not leave one detail to chance.
The sea does show up in this passage, but later. In verse 13 it gives up its dead. Where the dragon goes is the Abyss, the place the angel had the key to.
John never mentions a wilderness here. The angel comes down with a key and a chain, and the key is for the Abyss. That's where the dragon is thrown, and then it's shut and sealed.

Yes, baker. John says the angel sealed the Abyss over him "…so that he could not deceive the nations until the thousand years were complete." Deceiving the nations is what he can't do while he's sealed in there. Until the thousand years are complete, that's off the table.
It's a natural guess, but it isn't the word John uses. The text says the dragon is sealed away "…so that he could not deceive the nations…" Deceiving is the word that fits the blank.
John doesn't say anything about cursing here. He says the Abyss is sealed over the dragon "…so that he could not deceive the nations…" The word that fits is deceive.

Not quite, friend. John says the thousand years are not the end of the dragon's story. Right after saying he's sealed in until the thousand years are complete, he adds, "After that, he must be released for a brief period of time." So he doesn't stay sealed in for good.

Right, baker. The seal lasts until the thousand years are complete, and John says, "After that, he must be released for a brief period of time." The release comes up again in verse 7. So the dragon doesn't stay sealed in for good.
That's it. John sees the souls of those beheaded "…for their testimony of Jesus and for the word of God…" Their testimony was about Jesus, and it cost them. Jesus is named right there in the verse.

Moses was Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), and he's a big name in Scripture. John doesn't name him here, though. The text says these people were beheaded "…for their testimony of Jesus and for the word of God…"
Elijah was a prophet (1 Kings 18:36), and he's a big name too. But John doesn't mention him in this vision. These souls were beheaded "…for their testimony of Jesus and for the word of God…"

explanations.answer: They come to life and reign with Christ
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. John says, "…they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years." That's for the beheaded souls and for those who refused the beast and its mark. I think that's a hopeful thing to read after such a heavy picture.

explanations.answer: They rest under the altar a while longer
explanations.explanation: Souls under an altar do appear earlier in Revelation (Revelation 6:9). That's earlier in the book, though, and this is a different scene. In this passage John says something else about these ones. "…they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years."

explanations.answer: They stand guard over the sealed Abyss
explanations.explanation: John never gives them a guard post. The angel is the one who sealed the Abyss. What John says about these souls is that "…they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years."

That's right, friend. After telling us the rest of the dead wait, John says, "This is the first resurrection." Coming to life and reigning with Christ is what he's calling it. He uses a plain, direct word.
Harvest is a fine word, but John doesn't use it here. Verse 5 says, "This is the first resurrection." That's the word that fits the blank, straight from John.
John does get to a judgment, but later, at the great white throne in verses 11 to 15. Here in verse 5 he names something different. He says, "This is the first resurrection."

That's right. John says of those who share in the first resurrection, "The second death has no power over them…" Then he adds that they "…will be priests of God and of Christ…" Blessed and holy, like he said.

Not this time, friend. John says it plainly about those who share in the first resurrection: "The second death has no power over them…" So the statement matches what he wrote. The second death has no power over them.

explanations.answer: Priests of God and of Christ
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. John says, "…they will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with Him for a thousand years." They serve and they reign, both at once. John writes both in the same breath.
John doesn't call them prophets here. The text says they "…will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with Him for a thousand years." Priests is the word he uses.

explanations.answer: Guards at the gates of the city
explanations.explanation: There's a city later in this passage, the beloved city in verse 9. But John never puts these people on guard duty. He says they "…will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with Him for a thousand years."

That's it, friend. Satan goes out to deceive the nations "…to assemble them for battle." Gog and Magog are the names John gives here. The deceiving comes first, and the battle is what he gathers them for.

Building a tower is a different story, the one in Genesis where people said, "let us build for ourselves a city and a tower" (Genesis 11:4). John doesn't say that here. He says Satan deceives the nations "…to assemble them for battle."
That's a good guess, but John doesn't say it. The text says Satan goes out to deceive the nations "…to assemble them for battle." So battle is what they're gathered for.

explanations.answer: Fire comes down from heaven and consumes them
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. John says, "But fire came down from heaven and consumed them." The army surrounds the camp and the beloved city, and then the fire falls. John doesn't describe any fighting before that.

explanations.answer: The saints march out and drive them away
explanations.explanation: John never says the saints march out. He only says the army surrounds the camp of the saints and the beloved city. The next thing he reports is the fire. "But fire came down from heaven and consumed them."

explanations.answer: They turn around and run back home
explanations.explanation: John doesn't say the army turns around. After they surround the camp and the city, he says, "But fire came down from heaven and consumed them." That's what he reports happening to them.

This part is heavy, friend, so I'll go gently. The thousand years in this passage belong to the binding and the reign. About the lake of fire, John says, "There they will be tormented day and night forever and ever." So it doesn't end after a thousand years.

That's right, and I think this is a heavy verse. John says the devil, the beast and the false prophet "…will be tormented day and night forever and ever." He doesn't put a thousand years on it. The thousand years belong to the binding and the reign.

That's right, friend. John says, "Earth and heaven fled from His presence, and no place was found for them." There's the great white throne, and the One seated on it has that kind of presence. John gives the picture and moves on.
John doesn't mention angels fleeing here. What he says flees is "Earth and heaven…" And he adds that "…no place was found for them."
Kings of the earth aren't in this verse. John says that "Earth and heaven fled from His presence, and no place was found for them." So earth and heaven are what flee.
Yes, baker. John says, "…the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books." The books are opened, and one of them is the Book of Life. Deeds is the word John uses.
John doesn't say prayers here. He says "…the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books." The word that fits the blank is deeds.
Offerings aren't mentioned in this verse. John says "…the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books." Deeds is the word that fits.

That's right. John says, "The sea gave up its dead, and Death and Hades gave up their dead…" The sea isn't the only place the dead come from. Death and Hades give up theirs too, and each one is judged according to his deeds.

Not quite, friend. John says, "The sea gave up its dead, and Death and Hades gave up their dead…" So Death and Hades give up their dead too, along with the sea. And each one is judged according to his deeds.

Yes, baker. John writes, "Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death…" He gives the lake of fire that name himself. Remember, he said earlier the second death has no power over those who share in the first resurrection.
Not this time, friend. John does call it that. He writes, "This is the second death…" and says it's the lake of fire. So the statement matches the text.

explanations.answer: Anyone not written in the Book of Life
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. John writes, "…if anyone was found whose name was not written in the Book of Life, he was thrown into the lake of fire." Anyone whose name isn't found in that book is the one thrown in. I think it's a sobering way to end the passage.

explanations.answer: Anyone who stood before the throne
explanations.explanation: Everyone who stood before the throne does get judged. John says "…the dead, great and small…" stood there. But the one who is thrown into the lake of fire is anyone whose name was not written in the Book of Life.

explanations.answer: Anyone who had been great on the earth
explanations.explanation: John does say the dead who stand before the throne are "…great and small…" But he doesn't say greatness decides it. The one who is thrown into the lake of fire is anyone whose name was not written in the Book of Life.
